A server Script makes a zombie NPC chase a far-away target with a single call:
```lua
zombie.Humanoid:MoveTo(target.Position)
zombie.Humanoid.MoveToFinished:Wait()
print("arrived")
```
On long routes the zombie walks for a while, stops partway, prints "arrived" anyway, and it also walks straight into walls instead of going around them. Explain both problems and how to fix them.
answer_key: Humanoid:MoveTo times out after 8 seconds if the goal is not reached; MoveToFinished then fires with reached = false (the script ignores the reached argument)

MoveTo walks in a straight line with no obstacle avoidance; use PathfindingService (CreatePath, Path:ComputeAsync, check Status == Success, GetWaypoints) and move waypoint by waypoint, calling MoveTo for each (or re-calling MoveTo periodically to refresh the timeout)
Handle waypoints whose Action is Jump (make the humanoid jump) and recompute when Path.Blocked fires or the computation fails

responses.R1:
Problem 1: Humanoid:MoveTo has an 8-second timeout. If the goal isn't reached by then, the humanoid stops walking and MoveToFinished fires anyway, with reached = false. Your code ignores that argument, so it prints "arrived". Fix: `local reached = hum.MoveToFinished:Wait()` and check it. For long trips, call MoveTo again on each waypoint, which resets the timer.
Problem 2: MoveTo walks in a straight line and knows nothing about obstacles. Fix: use PathfindingService.
```lua
local path = PathfindingService:CreatePath({AgentRadius=2, AgentHeight=5, AgentCanJump=true})
local ok = pcall(path.ComputeAsync, path, root.Position, target.Position)
if ok and path.Status == Enum.PathStatus.Success then
  for _, wp in path:GetWaypoints() do
    if wp.Action == Enum.PathWaypointAction.Jump then hum.Jump = true end
    hum:MoveTo(wp.Position)
    if not hum.MoveToFinished:Wait() then break end -- recompute
  end
end
```
Also listen to path.Blocked and recompute the path. A moving target needs a fresh path every so often. Call root:SetNetworkOwner(nil) so the server owns the NPC and its movement doesn't stutter.

prompt: A ScreenGui in StarterGui holds a settings menu. Players toggle options (music off, a selected tab) and the LocalScript inside the ScreenGui stores them in local variables. Every time the player's character dies and respawns, the menu reverts to its defaults. Why, and what is the fix?
answer_key: ScreenGui.ResetOnSpawn defaults to true, so on each respawn the GUI is deleted and a fresh copy is cloned from StarterGui into PlayerGui, restarting its LocalScript and losing state

Fix: set ResetOnSpawn = false on the ScreenGui (a direct child of StarterGui is then cloned into PlayerGui only once and survives respawns), or keep the state outside the GUI (e.g. a script in StarterPlayerScripts, attributes, or the server)

Fix: set ResetOnSpawn = false on the settings ScreenGui (the script then runs once and state persists), or keep settings outside the GUI (a ModuleScript/client state in PlayerScripts or attributes on the Player) and re-apply on spawn. To persist across sessions, send the settings to the server (validated) and save them in a DataStore.

Fixes: (1) set ScreenGui.ResetOnSpawn = false so the GUI and its script stay alive, or (2) keep the settings somewhere that outlives the GUI: a ModuleScript or LocalScript under StarterPlayerScripts, or attributes on the Player, and re-apply them when the GUI is created. To keep settings across sessions, send them to the server (validated) and save them in a DataStore. Also don't parent long-lived state scripts under StarterCharacterScripts, which reset the same way.

prompt: In a LocalScript I play a sword-swing animation on my own character and every player sees it. In the same LocalScript I also play a waving animation on a shopkeeper NPC (a server-owned Model in Workspace with a Humanoid), but other players never see the NPC wave. For a second NPC, I created the Animator with Instance.new inside the LocalScript, and nobody else sees that one either. Explain the replication rules and the fix.
answer_key: Animations started on a client replicate only for that player's own character (or models the client has network ownership of); for other models such as server-owned NPCs, the animation must be loaded and played on the server to replicate
The Animator must be created on the server (or exist in the model already) and replicate to clients; an Animator created locally on the client does not replicate its tracks
Fix: play the NPC animations from a server Script via Animator:LoadAnimation(...):Play() (or fire a remote to every client and have each play it locally if it is purely cosmetic)

responses.R1: Animations replicate from the client only when the client is the authority for that Animator: a LocalScript can play animations on its own character (the player owns it, and the Animator was created by the server), and those replicate to everyone. For a server-owned NPC, animations played from a client stay local; nobody else sees them. An Animator created with Instance.new on the client exists only on that client, so nothing it plays replicates. Fix: play NPC animations from a server Script (Humanoid/AnimationController -> Animator:LoadAnimation(anim):Play()), with the Animator created on the server (or let the Humanoid create it server-side). If the client triggers the wave, fire a RemoteEvent and let the server validate and play it. Purely cosmetic local-only waves can stay client-side, but then each client must play them itself.
responses.R2: Animations replicate from the client only when the client is the one allowed to animate that rig: its own character (the Animator under its Humanoid/AnimationController that the server created). Animation tracks played by a client on a server-owned NPC stay local, so nobody else sees the wave. An Animator created with Instance.new on the client only exists on that client, so the server and other players never even see it, and nothing it plays can replicate. Fix: play NPC animations from the server: a server Script loads the Animation via npc.Humanoid.Animator:LoadAnimation(anim) and :Play(). Make sure the Animator exists on the server (create it server-side or include it in the model). If a client triggers the wave, fire a RemoteEvent and let the server play it. Also the animation asset must be owned by the experience owner/group.
responses.R3: Animations replicate from a client only when that client is the network owner of the rig: its own character, through Humanoid/AnimationController > Animator. That's why the sword swing replicates. The shopkeeper NPC belongs to the server, so animations a client plays on it stay local and nobody else sees them. For the second NPC, the Animator was made with Instance.new on the client, so it exists only on that client and doesn't replicate. Fix: play NPC animations from a server Script, using the Animator that the server created (or that ships in the model): `npc.Humanoid.Animator:LoadAnimation(anim):Play()`. Server-played animations replicate to everyone. Alternative: fire a RemoteEvent to all clients and have each client play it locally. Never create the Animator on the client. On the server, Humanoid:WaitForChild("Animator") or create it there. The animation asset must be owned by the experience owner (user or group), or it won't load.
responses.R4: Animation replication works through the Animator. Animations played from the client replicate only when the client has authority over that Animator: its own character, since it owns the character's network physics. A server-owned NPC isn't controlled by your client, so an animation you play on it stays local and only you see it. An Animator created with Instance.new on the client exists only on that client, so nothing replicates from it. Fix: play NPC animations from a server Script (Humanoid/AnimationController -> Animator:LoadAnimation(anim):Play()). Have the server create the Animator, or let the Humanoid create it. If the client triggers the wave, fire a RemoteEvent and have the server validate it and play the animation. Alternatively, have every client play it locally, for example by firing all clients. Keep playing the player's own character animations on the client: that is correct and they replicate. Never create Animators on the client for things that must replicate.
responses.R5:
Animation replication rule: animations played on a client replicate only for characters or models whose Animator that client owns. In practice that means the local player's own character, whose Animator was created by the server or by Roblox. So your sword swing replicates.
The shopkeeper NPC is owned by the server. Animations a client plays on it stay local, so only that player sees the wave.
An Animator created by Instance.new in a LocalScript exists only on that client. The server and other players never see the Animator, so nothing replicates.
Fix: play NPC animations from a server Script, using the Animator that exists on the server (`hum:FindFirstChildOfClass("Animator")` or one the server creates) with Animator:LoadAnimation(anim):Play(). That replicates to everyone. For purely cosmetic NPC idles you can instead have every client play the animation locally. Don't create Animators on the client for your own character either. Use the existing one under Humanoid.
responses.R6: Animations replicate only when played through an Animator the network model knows about. Your own character: the client owns it and the Animator is created by the server (Humanoid), so client-played animations on your own character replicate to everyone. The server-owned NPC: a client playing tracks on a server-owned Humanoid/Animator is local-only; it doesn't replicate. The NPC whose Animator you created with Instance.new on the client: that Animator exists only on your client, so nothing replicates. Fix: play NPC animations from a server Script (Animator created on the server, e.g. Humanoid's default or server-side Instance.new), triggered via a validated RemoteEvent if a client action starts it, or deliberately play them on every client (FireAllClients) if purely cosmetic. Always load via Animator:LoadAnimation, never Humanoid:LoadAnimation, and only create Animators on the server.

prompt: Three sound bugs in one game: (1) a Sound placed directly in Workspace for a barrel explosion is heard at full volume by every player across the whole map; (2) a Sound inside a siren Part goes silent once players are a moderate distance away, but the designer wants it audible much further; (3) a script does `siren.Loaded:Wait()` before playing and sometimes hangs forever. Explain each and fix.
answer_key: (1) A Sound not parented to a BasePart or Attachment is global (same volume everywhere); parent it to the barrel part or an Attachment at the explosion to make it positional
(2) For positional sounds the audible range is controlled by RollOffMaxDistance (with RollOffMinDistance and RollOffMode shaping the falloff); raise RollOffMaxDistance
(3) Loaded does not fire if the sound has already loaded, so check Sound.IsLoaded first and only wait on Loaded when it is false

responses.R1:
(1) A Sound whose parent is Workspace (or SoundService or the GUI) has no position, so it plays globally at full volume for everyone. Fix: parent it to the barrel's Part or an Attachment so it becomes positional, and set RollOffMaxDistance. Or have the server clone it into the barrel and Play it there, then clean it up (Debris, or Ended -> Destroy).
(2) Positional volume fades with distance according to RollOffMode and RollOffMinDistance/RollOffMaxDistance. Past RollOffMaxDistance the sound is silent. Fix: raise RollOffMaxDistance (and RollOffMinDistance) and use RollOffMode Inverse/InverseTapered, or Linear for a predictable fade. Optionally add a second, global siren on the client.
(3) Loaded fires only once. If the sound has already loaded before you call Wait, the event never fires again and the script hangs. Fix: `if not siren.IsLoaded then siren.Loaded:Wait() end` (ideally with a timeout), or just call Play(), which starts the sound when it loads. You can also preload with ContentProvider:PreloadAsync.
responses.R2: (1) A Sound parented to Workspace (or any non-positional parent like SoundService) is non-positional (2D): everyone hears it at full volume. Parent it to a Part or Attachment at the barrel position so it is 3D; clone and play a fresh sound per explosion (Debris/Ended cleanup). (2) Positional sounds attenuate by RollOffMinDistance / RollOffMaxDistance and RollOffMode. Raise RollOffMaxDistance (and RollOffMinDistance for the full-volume radius), use Linear/InverseTapered for a controlled fall-off, and raise Volume if needed. (3) Loaded only fires once when loading completes; if the sound is already loaded (IsLoaded true) before you wait, the event never fires again, so it hangs. Use `if not siren.IsLoaded then siren.Loaded:Wait() end`, or just call Play() (it plays once loaded); optionally ContentProvider:PreloadAsync. Also check the SoundId is valid/permitted, or Loaded never fires.
responses.R3:
(1) A Sound parented to Workspace or a service (not a Part or Attachment) is non-positional: it plays globally at full volume for everyone. Fix: parent it to the barrel Part or an Attachment so it is 3D and attenuates with distance. Set RollOffMode and RollOffMinDistance/RollOffMaxDistance.
(2) Positional sounds fade according to RollOffMode, RollOffMinDistance and RollOffMaxDistance. Inverse rolloff, the default, drops quickly. Fix: raise RollOffMinDistance (the full-volume radius) and RollOffMaxDistance (for example 300-500). Use Linear or InverseTapered so it stays audible further out. Volume alone won't carry it.
(3) Loaded fires only once, when loading finishes. If the sound is already loaded when Wait() is called, the event never fires again, so the script hangs. Fix: `if not siren.IsLoaded then siren.Loaded:Wait() end` (optionally with a timeout), or preload with ContentProvider:PreloadAsync. Also check that the SoundId is valid and that the place has permission to use the asset.
responses.R4: (1) A Sound is positional (3D) only when parented to a BasePart or Attachment. Parented directly to Workspace (or SoundService) it is global, same volume for everyone. Fix: parent it to a part/Attachment at the barrel, with sensible RollOffMinDistance (~20-40) and RollOffMaxDistance (~300-600). (2) Audibility range is governed by RollOffMinDistance (full volume radius, default 10), RollOffMaxDistance (default 10000) and RollOffMode (Inverse default falls off fast). Raise RollOffMinDistance, set RollOffMaxDistance to the range wanted, and use Linear/InverseTapered for a gentle, predictable falloff (InverseTapered avoids the cliff). Fix: if not siren.IsLoaded then waitWithTimeout(siren.Loaded, 5) end, then play; or just call :Play() (it plays when ready) / use ContentProvider:PreloadAsync.

prompt:
A gun LocalScript does:
```lua
local dir = (mouseHit - head.Position).Unit
local result = workspace:Raycast(head.Position, dir)
print(result.Instance.Name)
```
It almost always errors with "attempt to index nil with 'Instance'", and when it does hit something it is often the player's own body. Diagnose and fix.
answer_key: The direction vector's length is the ray's length, so a .Unit direction only casts 1 stud; multiply the unit direction by the desired range (e.g. dir * 300)
Workspace:Raycast returns nil when nothing is hit, so check the result before reading .Instance
Pass RaycastParams with FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude and FilterDescendantsInstances = {player.Character} to ignore the shooter

responses.R1:
workspace:Raycast's direction is the full ray vector, not just a direction: a .Unit vector is only 1 stud long, so it almost never hits anything and Raycast returns nil, then `result.Instance` errors. And with no filter, the ray starts inside your own head/character and hits it. Fix:
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {player.Character}
local dir = (mouseHit - head.Position).Unit * 500
local result = workspace:Raycast(head.Position, dir, params)
if result then
  print(result.Instance.Name, result.Position)
end
```
Always nil-check the result. For a real gun, also do the authoritative raycast on the server (validate origin, distance and rate) rather than trusting the client's hit.

workspace:Raycast's direction is a vector whose length IS the ray distance. .Unit makes it 1 stud long, so it nearly always misses and returns nil; you then index nil. And the ray starts inside the head, so it hits your own character. Fix:

params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude

Always nil-check the result. For a real gun, also do the authoritative raycast/validation on the server, not just the client.

prompt: A shop button has a hover effect (TweenService tweens BackgroundTransparency to 0.2 over 0.3 s on MouseEnter) and a click flash (a separate tween of BackgroundTransparency to 0 and back). When players click while the hover tween is still running, the hover effect stops halfway and the button ends in odd states. Why does this happen and how should the code be structured?
answer_key: Two tweens on the same property of the same object conflict: the earlier tween is cancelled and overwritten by the most recently played one

Fix: keep a reference to the active tween per button and Cancel it before playing a new one (or chain via Completed), or have the effects animate different properties / objects (e.g. a child frame or UIStroke) so they don't share a property

responses.R1:
Two tweens on the same property of the same instance conflict. Starting the click tween cancels the hover tween that is still running (the newest tween wins). The hover's Completed then fires with Cancelled, and any follow-up logic runs from a half-finished value. Restoring "back" to a value captured mid-tween leaves the button in odd states. Structure: keep one source of truth for the button's state (hovered, pressed) and one active tween per property. Store the current tween, Cancel() it before you create a new one, and always tween toward a target computed from the state, not from the current value:
```lua
local current
local function go(t, props) if current then current:Cancel() end current = TweenService:Create(btn, TweenInfo.new(t), props) current:Play() end
local function target() return hovered and 0.2 or 0.5 end
btn.MouseEnter:Connect(function() hovered=true go(0.3,{BackgroundTransparency=target()}) end)
btn.MouseLeave:Connect(function() hovered=false go(0.3,{BackgroundTransparency=target()}) end)
btn.Activated:Connect(function() go(0.05,{BackgroundTransparency=0}) task.delay(0.05,function() go(0.15,{BackgroundTransparency=target()}) end) end)
```
Better still, animate the flash on a separate property or a child overlay frame (or a UIScale) so it never fights the hover tween.
responses.R2:
Two tweens on the same property of the same instance conflict. When a new tween starts on BackgroundTransparency, Roblox cancels the earlier tween on that property. The hover tween stops partway, and the click tween's 'back' value is taken from a snapshot of the half-finished state. Unordered MouseLeave/MouseEnter events then leave the button in odd states. Structure it as a small state machine with one owner per property: track state (hovered, pressed) and one current tween; cancel it before starting another, and always tween to the target computed from the state, not to relative or snapshot values.
```lua
local current
local hovered = false
local function goTo(t, time)
  if current then current:Cancel() end
  current = TweenService:Create(btn, TweenInfo.new(time), {BackgroundTransparency = t})
  current:Play()
end
btn.MouseEnter:Connect(function() hovered = true; goTo(0.2, 0.3) end)
btn.MouseLeave:Connect(function() hovered = false; goTo(0.5, 0.3) end)
btn.Activated:Connect(function()
  goTo(0, 0.05)
  current.Completed:Wait()
  goTo(hovered and 0.2 or 0.5, 0.15)
end)
```
Or animate the flash on a different property or object (for example a UIStroke or an overlay frame) so the two effects never compete.
responses.R3:
Only one tween can control a given property of an instance at a time. When a new tween on BackgroundTransparency starts, the hover tween still running on that property is cancelled. It stays wherever it stopped (Completed fires with Cancelled), and nothing restores it. When the flash ends it goes to its own fixed value, not to the current hover state. So the hover and flash tweens fight and leave inconsistent end states.
Structure it as a small state machine:
- Track the state (hovered: bool, pressed: bool).
- Write one function that computes the target value from that state and plays the tween, and keep a reference to the current tween. Cancel it before starting a new one.
- MouseEnter/MouseLeave set hovered and call the function. Click plays the flash and, when it completes, tweens back to the target for the current state, not to a hardcoded value.
- Or animate different properties so they don't conflict: hover on BackgroundTransparency, click on UIScale.Scale or a separate overlay Frame.
Also debounce clicks, and do purchase logic on the server, not in the animation.

prompt: Write a short server-side Luau snippet that makes every part tagged "Lava" kill players who touch it, including Lava parts that are added later at runtime (e.g. cloned in during a round), and cleans up when a part loses the tag or is removed. State the key rules.
answer_key: Use CollectionService:GetTagged("Lava") for parts that already exist AND CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal("Lava") for later ones (the added signal does not fire for instances already tagged)

Store each part's Touched connection and disconnect it in CollectionService:GetInstanceRemovedSignal("Lava") (fires when the tag is removed or the instance leaves the DataModel); run on the server (server tags replicate to clients)

responses.R1:
```lua
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local conns = {}
local function onAdded(part)
  if not part:IsA("BasePart") or conns[part] then return end
  conns[part] = part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    local char = hit:FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model")
    local hum = char and char:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if hum and Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(char) and hum.Health > 0 then
      hum.Health = 0
    end
  end)
end
local function onRemoved(part)
  if conns[part] then conns[part]:Disconnect(); conns[part] = nil end
end
CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal("Lava"):Connect(onAdded)
CollectionService:GetInstanceRemovedSignal("Lava"):Connect(onRemoved)
for _, p in CollectionService:GetTagged("Lava") do onAdded(p) end
```
Rules: run it on the server (a Script in ServerScriptService), so the kill is authoritative. Connect the Added/Removed signals AND loop over the existing GetTagged parts so nothing is missed. The removed signal also fires when a tagged instance leaves the DataModel (is destroyed), so a table keyed by part plus Disconnect avoids leaks. Guard against non-parts and duplicate connections. CanTouch must be true.

prompt: Write a minimal Luau ProcessReceipt handler for a developer product that gives 500 coins (coins are saved in a DataStore). Explain the key rules that prevent lost or double-granted purchases.
answer_key: Set MarketplaceService.ProcessReceipt only once, in a single server-side Script; it must handle all developer products (look up by receiptInfo.ProductId, player by receiptInfo.PlayerId)
Return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted only after the coins were successfully granted/saved; return NotProcessedYet if the player is not in the server or the grant/save failed
Make it idempotent: record receiptInfo.PurchaseId (e.g. via DataStore UpdateAsync) and skip granting if that PurchaseId was already processed, since the receipt can be delivered again
A NotProcessedYet receipt is not retried on a timer: the callback runs again when the player makes another product purchase or rejoins a server of the experience

responses.R1:
```lua
local MPS = game:GetService("MarketplaceService")
local DSS = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DSS:GetDataStore("PlayerData")
local PRODUCT = 123456
MPS.ProcessReceipt = function(info)
  if info.ProductId ~= PRODUCT then return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet end
  local key = "Player_" .. info.PlayerId
  local ok, err = pcall(function()
    store:UpdateAsync(key, function(data)
      data = data or {Coins = 0, Receipts = {}}
      data.Receipts = data.Receipts or {}
      if data.Receipts[info.PurchaseId] then return data end -- already granted
      data.Coins += 500
      data.Receipts[info.PurchaseId] = true
      return data
    end)
  end)
  if not ok then warn(err); return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet end
  local plr = game.Players:GetPlayerByUserId(info.PlayerId)
  if plr then -- update the in-memory and leaderstats copy here
  end
  return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted
end
```
Rules:
- Set ProcessReceipt exactly once, in a single server Script.
- Return PurchaseGranted only after the grant is durably saved.
- On any failure, or an unknown product, return NotProcessedYet. Roblox retries later, including on the player's next join, so never error out.
- Make the grant idempotent by recording PurchaseId atomically with the coins in the same UpdateAsync. That prevents double grants.
- Don't require the player to be in the server to save.
- In practice, cap the stored receipt history to recent IDs.

prompt: Players can type a custom message that is shown on a sign above their plot, visible to everyone in the server (and it stays after the author leaves). Write the server-side Luau for filtering the text before displaying it and state the key rules.
answer_key: Filter on the server with TextService:FilterStringAsync(text, authorUserId) wrapped in pcall (it yields and can throw; the author must be in the server)
For text every user can see, display TextFilterResult:GetNonChatStringForBroadcastAsync() (GetNonChatStringForUserAsync is for text only one specific user sees; GetChatForUserAsync is deprecated)
If filtering fails, do not show the text (show nothing / a placeholder); never display the raw unfiltered string

responses.R1:
```lua
local TextService = game:GetService("TextService")
local Chat = game:GetService("Chat")
local SetSign = game.ReplicatedStorage.SetSign -- RemoteEvent
local last = {}
SetSign.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, text)
  if typeof(text) ~= "string" or #text == 0 or #text > 100 then return end
  if last[player] and os.clock() - last[player] < 5 then return end -- rate limit
  last[player] = os.clock()
  local ok, result = pcall(TextService.FilterStringAsync, TextService, text, player.UserId, Enum.TextFilterContext.PublicChat)
  if not ok then return end -- on failure show nothing / keep the old text
  local ok2, filtered = pcall(result.GetNonChatStringForBroadcastAsync, result)
  if not ok2 then return end
  getPlotSign(player).SurfaceGui.TextLabel.Text = filtered
end)
```
Rules:
- Filter on the server only, with the author's UserId. Text from the client is untrusted, so validate its type and length.
- Text seen by everyone uses GetNonChatStringForBroadcastAsync. Text for one viewer uses GetNonChatStringForUserAsync(viewerId).
- Wrap filtering in pcall. If it fails, show nothing or placeholder text, never the raw text.
- Store the raw text but always re-filter before display. If you persist it, re-filter when you reload it.
- Never display unfiltered text, even briefly. Rate-limit submissions.

answer_key: UnreliableRemoteEvent does not guarantee delivery (lost events are not resent) or ordering, so it suits ephemeral or continuously updated data like the cosmetic/state updates

responses.R1: Yes, for the continuous, cosmetic stream. Steering, throttle and exhaust effects sent 20 times a second are fine to lose, because the next update replaces the last one. Payloads over about 1,000 bytes are dropped, so keep them small: pack numbers, for example with buffers or quantized values. When throttled, extra messages are dropped, not queued. Messages arriving with no handler connected are discarded. API: FireServer/FireClient/FireAllClients and OnServerEvent/OnClientEvent, the same as RemoteEvent. Keep lap completion, finish order, and any on/off state on a reliable RemoteEvent, because a dropped one can't be recovered. Validate lap events on the server with checkpoints, never trust the client.

prompt: Server-controlled boss NPCs (unanchored, moved by Humanoids) stutter whenever players walk near them, and the boss's Touched-based damage can be faked by exploiters. What is going on with physics ownership and what should we do?
answer_key: By default network ownership is automatic: the engine hands unanchored assemblies to nearby players' clients, and ownership changes cause hitches; call SetNetworkOwner(nil) on the NPC's parts/root so the server owns the NPC
When a client owns a part, Roblox cannot verify its physics, so client-owned parts' positions and Touched events can be faked; important hit detection must be validated on the server

Fix: call `boss.HumanoidRootPart:SetNetworkOwner(nil)` (server) on the boss's assembly after spawning, which pins simulation to the server and stops the handoffs (SetNetworkOwnershipAuto() reverts). For damage, don't rely on Touched from client-simulated parts: do server-side hit detection (spatial queries like workspace:GetPartBoundsInBox/Radius or raycasts at attack time with OverlapParams), with cooldowns, range checks and server-tracked health. Also anchor parts that don't need physics.

The handoff and its round trip cause the stutter and rubber-banding. That client also simulates the boss, so an exploiter who owns it can teleport or fling it, and fake Touched events: physics Touched for parts the client owns is decided by that client. Fix: after parenting the boss into Workspace, call `if root:CanSetNetworkOwnership() then root:SetNetworkOwner(nil) end` on the HumanoidRootPart (ownership is per assembly, and anchored parts error). Re-assert ownership after rigs change (ragdolls, new welds). Don't base damage on Touched alone. Do hit detection on the server: Workspace:GetPartBoundsInBox/GetPartsInPart or raycasts during the attack window, sanity-check distance and cooldowns, and apply damage only on the server. Never accept client-reported hits without range and timing checks. Trade-off: server-owned NPCs react to player pushes with a round-trip delay, which is fine for bosses. Collision groups can stop players from pushing them.

Damage: don't rely on Touched (fires from the owner's simulation and can be spoofed/unreliable); do server-side hit detection - spatial queries (GetPartBoundsInBox/Radius or raycasts) from the boss's attack at the attack moment, with cooldowns and distance checks. prompt: Our server spends most of its frame time computing line-of-sight raycasts for 60 turrets every Heartbeat. We want to use Parallel Luau. Describe how to structure it and what the restrictions are.
answer_key: Put the scripts under Actor instances (e.g. one actor per turret or group of turrets); only Actor descendants run in parallel
Switch to parallel with task.desynchronize() (or connect with RBXScriptSignal:ConnectParallel) for the read-only raycast work

Writing instance properties / modifying the DataModel is not allowed in parallel, so call task.synchronize() before applying results (e.g. rotating the turret, dealing damage); require cannot be called while desynchronized; share data via SharedTable or Actor messages

responses.R1: Structure: put each batch of turrets (or each turret) under its own Actor (Actor instance containing the turret model and a Script), or one Actor per N turrets to keep overhead low. In each Actor's script, connect with `RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel(function() ... end)` (or task.desynchronize()). Do the expensive work in parallel: read positions, workspace:Raycast (raycasts and spatial queries are parallel-safe), compute target/angle. Then call `task.synchronize()` before writing results back (rotating the turret, firing, changing properties, firing remotes), or send results to a coordinator via Actor messages (SendMessage/BindToMessageParallel) or SharedTable. Restrictions: in the parallel (desynchronized) phase you can read the DataModel but cannot modify instances (except few safe ones), and only call APIs marked parallel-safe (read-safe/safe); no yielding functions there; each Actor's scripts have separate Luau VMs, so module state isn't shared (use SharedTable/messages); changes only apply in serial phase. Profile with MicroProfiler; only parallelize if per-turret work is heavy enough to beat the overhead.
responses.R2: Structure: put each group of turrets under an Actor (for example 60 turrets in roughly 4-8 Actors, or one per turret). The script inside the Actor connects with ConnectParallel to RunService.Heartbeat (or calls task.desynchronize()), then reads state and runs workspace:Raycast for its turrets in parallel. It stores results in local tables. Then task.synchronize() (or a later serial phase) applies the effects: rotating the turret, firing, damage, remotes. Use Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessage to pass targets in. SharedTable can share read-mostly data between Actors. Restrictions: in a desynchronized (parallel) phase you can read most properties and call thread-safe APIs (Raycast, GetPartBoundsInBox and similar spatial queries are safe), but you cannot write properties of instances outside your Actor, create or destroy instances, fire remotes, or call unsafe APIs; switch to serial for that. Each Actor has its own Lua VM, so modules are required separately per Actor and globals/state are not shared. Use SharedTable or messages instead. Parallel work only pays off when there is enough work to split. Reduce work as well: run line-of-sight at 5-10 Hz per turret staggered across frames, cull by distance first, and reuse RaycastParams. Profile with the MicroProfiler to confirm the speedup.
responses.R3: Split the turrets across Actors. Use about 16 to 64 Actors in total, each owning a group of turrets, not one Actor per turret. Put a Script under each Actor. In it: `RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel(function() ... end)`, or call task.desynchronize() inside a serial connection. In the parallel phase, read positions and run workspace:Raycast for each turret. Raycasts and reading properties are parallel-safe. Store the results in local tables. Then call task.synchronize() and apply the effects (rotate the turret, fire, deal damage, create instances) in the serial phase. Restrictions: writing most properties, creating, destroying or reparenting instances, firing remotes, and calling most yielding or unsafe APIs aren't allowed in parallel, and they error. Check each API's thread safety: Unsafe / Read Parallel / Local Safe / Safe. Each Actor gets its own copy of every required module, so module state isn't shared. Share data through SharedTable (SharedTableRegistry:GetSharedTable). Use SharedTable.increment for counters, never read-modify-write, and keep SharedTable.update functions pure. Or use Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessageParallel, but sent tables are copied in full, so keep messages small. task.desynchronize errors outside an Actor. Instances a script modifies should belong to its Actor. Also reduce the work: stagger checks over several frames, skip turrets with no target in range, use RaycastParams filters, and check the gains in the MicroProfiler.
responses.R4: Put each turret's logic in an Actor: one Actor per turret (or batches, e.g. 6 Actors each handling 10 turrets) with a Script inside. Store results in local tables, then call task.synchronize() before writing to the DataModel (rotating the turret, setting properties, firing remotes, damaging Humanoids). Communicate via Actor:SendMessage / BindToMessageParallel or SharedTable. Restrictions: in the desynchronized phase you can read most properties but cannot write instance properties, create/destroy/parent instances, or call most yielding/unsafe APIs (only those marked Parallel Safe/Read Safe); scripts in different Actors don't share Luau state (each Actor has its own VM; module requires are separate copies), so use SharedTable or messages; instances must be descendants of the Actor to be modified by it safely. Batch work so each Actor gets enough to amortize overhead, and profile with the MicroProfiler. Reducing frequency (e.g. raycast at 10 Hz, stagger turrets) helps too.
responses.R5: Put turret logic under Actors: e.g. split 60 turrets across several Actors (a few per core, e.g. 4-8 Actors, each with a Script handling its turrets) rather than one script. In each script: RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel(function() ... end) (or task.desynchronize()). In the parallel phase, read positions/attributes and call workspace:Raycast / Blockcast / GetPartBoundsInBox (thread-safe reads), and compute results into local tables. Then task.synchronize() and apply writes (rotate turrets, fire, set properties, fire remotes) in the serial phase. Restrictions: most property writes, creating/parenting/destroying instances, and many APIs are not allowed in parallel (check each member's thread-safety tag) - writes error until you synchronize. Each Actor has its own Lua VM: module state is not shared (require gives a separate copy), so share data via Actor messages (SendMessage/BindToMessage, args are copied), attributes, or SharedTable (SharedTable.increment is atomic; SharedTable.update may run multiple times, keep it pure). Also reduce work first: profile with MicroProfiler, raycast at lower rates, skip turrets with no nearby targets.
responses.R6:
Structure:
- Put each turret, or a group of turrets (for example 60 turrets split over 6-12 Actors), under its own Actor with a script inside. Scripts within the same Actor run sequentially, so you need several Actors.
- In each Actor, connect with `RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel(fn)`, or call `task.desynchronize()`.

- In the parallel phase you can't create, parent or destroy instances or set most properties. Unsafe API calls error.
- No `require` in parallel.
- Each Actor has its own Luau VM, so module state isn't shared. Messages are copied and can't contain functions.

- Don't desynchronize and synchronize several times per frame per turret.
